hero.title: Planning How The UpSkilling Labs Will Evolve
hero.summary: Logic model view of envisioned improvements to The UpSkilling Labs program and growth. Over time these improvements lend to shared knowledge and adaptable structures that can benefit new communities, volunteers, and learners.
hero.howToRead: Read left to right. Each column leads to the next: what we put in, what we do, what we can count, then what we intend to change within 12 months, in 1 to 3 years, and in 3 years or more. Every item names the workstream it belongs to. Choose a workstream to highlight its items.

items.text: Builders in residence, who give 4 to 6 hours a week to research and build.
Maintainers, who keep the work going between Build Cycles.
Learning content contributors, who create and share learning content.
Coding agents that handle clerical work so volunteers can do the thinking.
OLOS, The Labs' open-source platform, and the region's own copy of it.
GitHub, where research, code and records are kept in public.
Communication tools: Slack, Luma and email.
Records from past Build Cycles.
Learning content The Labs has already delivered.
Funding from [funders].
Create an ecosystem map of The Labs.
Create a glossary of important terms.
Identify key learning content for different stages of user engagement.
Create an improved version of OLOS.
Make a plan for syncing multiple communication channels.
Make a plan for developing a standardized approach to content delivery.
Make a plan for developing the skillsets and training that new learning content contributors need.
Provide resources and lessons learned to builders in residence.
Recruit new volunteers.
Promote public events.

Volunteers and staff share one picture of the ecosystem and use the same words for it.
The team knows which learning content serves each stage of engagement.
People at The Labs use the improved version of OLOS in their work.
The team has agreed plans for communication channels, content delivery and contributor training.
Builders in residence start from maintainers' resources and lessons, not from scratch.
New volunteers join, and more people come to public events.
Slack, Luma and email stay in sync, so people find the same information wherever they look.
Learning content is delivered in one standard way, whoever made it.
Trained learning content contributors add new content on their own.
Learning content and process resources start collecting in one shared place.
Each Build Cycle starts from the records and lessons of the one before.
Other regions adopt OLOS changes made here.
New regions start Labs from shared tools and lessons, not from scratch.
A volunteer-led way of upskilling that funders and partners can back with confidence.
A master repository holds The Labs' learning content and process resources.
A self-service learning platform lets people find and use learning content on their own.

indicators.intro: Sample measures for each outcome horizon. The team confirms which ones it already tracks and sets targets from a baseline.

horizons.title: Short term
items: [X]% of participants who say they can use a coding agent to build something, before and after a Cycle.
[X]% of contributors who take part in a second Cycle.
[#] changes running in the region's OLOS with at least three regular users.
[#] partners who have hosted, mentored or brought a problem.

horizons.title: Medium term
items: [X]% of past participants reporting a new job, course or civic role that used what they learned, at 12 months.
[#] pods led by people who started as contributors.
[#] changes from this region accepted into the main OLOS project.
[#] times research or write-ups are reused by other pods or regions.

horizons.title: Long term
items: [#] Greater Washington residents who have completed a Cycle.
[#] community problems with a working response still in use after a year.
[#] new regions running their own copy of OLOS.
Share of The Labs' budget from [#] recurring funders and partners.

assumptions: Neighbors will give 4 to 6 hours a week for six weeks when the work is real and the people using it are close by.
Coding agents let people without a coding background build working software.
Partners will lend space, time or expertise when they can see where it fits.
Keeping the work in public makes it easier for others to reuse.
external: How fast AI tools change, and what they cost.
Volunteer capacity around jobs, family and the calendar.
Funding cycles and what funders are prioritizing.
Policies at partner institutions about space, data and AI use.
